questions.learningObjective: Explain why a memorial's meaning cannot be separated from its site
questions.stem: Drafting the interpretive text for a memorial hall, you must explain why the site cannot be separated from the work.

answer.exemplar: A memorial draws its force from where it stands, because the site carries the record that the object refers to. The ground, the scale of the space and the relation of the building to the streets that lead to it all instruct the visitor about what happened and how large it was, and none of that is carried by the materials themselves. Moving the memorial elsewhere preserves the names but empties the address, which is why the choice of place is part of the argument rather than a practical detail.

questions.explanation: A memorial's site carries the event it refers to and shapes how the work is encountered, so siting is part of its meaning. Moving it can keep the material and lose the address.

questions.learningObjective: Compare the audience a mural addresses with a gallery's
questions.stem: Writing the curatorial appendix, you must explain how a mural's audience differs from a gallery's.

answer.exemplar: A mural is addressed to a public that has not come to see it. It is met on the way to somewhere else, usually at a glance and often without stopping, and it must therefore carry its argument in a form legible at speed and from a distance, across a surface shared with advertising and street language. Neither audience is more attentive by nature; they are different contracts.

questions.explanation: A mural addresses people in transit with no intention of looking, so brevity and legibility condition its argument. A gallery visitor has chosen to attend, a different contract rather than a better one.

questions.learningObjective: Set out how a photomontage argues through juxtaposition
questions.stem: Explaining the planning decision to a client who wants one clear message, you must set out how a photomontage argues.

answer.exemplar: A photomontage argues by juxtaposition. It takes images that were made separately, for different purposes, and sets them together so that the relation between them becomes the subject: a raised hand placed beside a factory gate, a headline placed over a crowd. Because the composite has never existed in the world, the relation it asserts is not found in any source but produced by the arrangement, which is why such images can propose a link that photographs of events cannot make on their own.

questions.explanation: A photomontage produces its claim by placing separately made images in a relation no source contains. That is why it can argue a link between things never photographed together.

answer.exemplar: The video form adds the dimension of time to a sequence of images. questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a documentary claim is a claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain why documentary images assert rather than merely record
questions.stem: Writing the conservation note for the archive, you must explain why documentary images make claims rather than merely record.

answer.exemplar: A documentary image is made under conditions that always exclude something: a particular angle, a moment chosen by the shutter, a subject selected by the photographer, and a caption that tells the viewer how to take it. The result is a claim about the world that can be assessed against other evidence, and the claim is stronger when those conditions are made visible. It is the openness of the claim to checking, not the presence of the camera, that gives documentary work its authority and its capacity to be wrong.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How an archive photograph frames its subject
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how much of an archive shows other subjects
questions.stem: An index of 1,250 photographs lists 320 shots of the harbour, and you must calculate how many show other subjects.
questions.explanation: Subtracting 320 harbour photographs from 1,250 gives 930 on other subjects. The balance matters because an archive's silence about a subject is a framing, not an absence of record.
questions.hint: Subtract the harbour group from the index.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Assess a memorial site chosen for what it enables

stimulus.body: A memorial is proposed for a square that carries no historical connection to the events it will commemorate. The architects' report notes that the square is the only space in the district large enough for gatherings of the size expected, and that the surrounding streets would have to be closed on the day of the ceremony.

questions.stem: Reviewing the commissioning notes for a memorial to be placed in a square with no historical link to the events.

options.text: The site is impossible, since a memorial is meaningless anywhere except where the events happened.
options.misconception: requires a memorial to stand on the event's own ground

options.text: The site can be chosen for what it makes possible, since a square can be made into a place of gathering.
The site is convenient, since the crowd size and street closures are the practical points.
options.misconception: reduces the choice of site to logistical considerations

options.text: The site is symbolic, since any open ground carries the same meaning as the original location.
options.misconception: treats all open ground as equivalent in meaning

questions.explanation: A site can be chosen for what it enables, since a square that can gather people becomes part of how the event is remembered. Only original ground, logistics and interchangeable ground each misdescribe the choice.
questions.hint: Ask what the new site allows to happen.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Separate the record a monument fixes from the public it addresses
questions.stem: Comparing two accounts of what a monument is for, you must separate the record from the address.

options.text: The record is the address, since the names are the only way a monument can speak at all.
options.misconception: reduces a monument's public work to its inscription

options.text: The record and the address are one thing, since a monument always speaks to the people it names.
options.misconception: assumes a monument addresses only those it names

options.text: The record is the history it fixes in stone; the address is the public it speaks to now.
Neither matters, since a monument's meaning is settled once its stone is carved.
options.misconception: treats meaning as fixed at the moment of carving

questions.explanation: A monument fixes a record in durable material and also addresses a public with no part in the history it records, and both are part of what it does. Naming only, inscription only and finality collapse that distinction.
questions.hint: Ask what the stone says and who hears it.
